slides.title: Saying hello
slides.text: Just say hi and tell them your name. That's a great way to start a new friendship.

slides.title: Sharing your toys
slides.text: Let your friend play with your toy for a bit. Sharing shows your friend that you are kind.

slides.title: Taking turns
slides.text: Take turns on the swing or in a game. That way, everyone gets a fair chance to play.

slides.title: Asking someone to play
slides.text: Ask a friend, 'Do you want to play?' It's a simple way to start having fun together.

slides.title: Being kind when someone's sad
slides.text: If a friend is sad, sit next to them. Ask them softly, 'Are you okay right now?'

slides.title: Saying sorry
slides.text: If you hurt a friend, say you are sorry. Then work together to help make it right.

slides.title: Including others
slides.text: If someone is playing alone, ask them to join. Including them can make their whole day better.

slides.title: Being a good listener friend
slides.text: Look at your friend when they are talking. Good listening shows your friend that you care.

slides.title: What makes a good friend
slides.text: A good friend is kind, fair, and helpful. A good friend shares and listens to you.

slides.title: Meeting friends somewhere new
slides.text: At a new school, say hi to someone first. New friends are often easier to find than you think.

slides.title: Giving compliments
slides.text: Tell a friend something nice, like 'I like your drawing.' Kind words can make a friend feel really happy.

slides.title: Helping a friend
slides.text: If a friend needs help, go help them. Good friends always take care of each other.

quiz.question: What should you do if you hurt a friend?

quiz.question: What's a kind thing to do if someone is playing alone?
choices: Invite them to join your game
Leave them by themselves
quiz.explanation: Including someone who's alone is a caring way to make a new friend.

quiz.question: What makes someone a good listener friend?
choices: Paying attention when a friend is talking
Only listening when it's convenient for you
quiz.explanation: Real listening means paying attention, which makes friends feel valued.

quiz.question: What does a good friend do?
choices: Share and listen to you
Ignore you and never share
quiz.explanation: Good friends are kind, fair, and helpful to each other.

quiz.question: What can you do at a new school?
choices: Say hi to someone first
Hide and talk to no one
quiz.explanation: Saying hi first is an easy way to meet a new friend.

quiz.question: What can kind words do for a friend?
choices: Make them feel happy
Make them feel bad
quiz.explanation: A kind compliment can brighten a friend's whole day.

slides.title: Finding common interests
slides.text: Friendships often start with something you both enjoy, like a game, a sport, or a show. Noticing what you have in common can turn a simple conversation into a real friendship.

slides.title: Joining a group at recess
slides.text: Walking up to a group and asking 'Can I play too?' takes some courage. Most groups are happy to include someone new, so it's worth asking.

slides.title: Being a good sport
slides.text: Whether you win or lose, staying friendly and saying 'good game' matters. It shows your friends that you care about having fun, not just winning.

slides.title: Keeping your promises
slides.text: When you tell a friend you'll do something, like saving them a seat, follow through. Keeping your word, even when it's tempting not to, builds real trust.

slides.title: Handling small disagreements
slides.text: Friends don't always agree, but calmly talking it out usually works better than staying mad. If you disagree about a game, try suggesting a fair compromise.

slides.title: Not gossiping about friends
slides.text: Talking behind a friend's back can hurt their trust in you if it gets back to them. It's usually better, though harder, to say what's bothering you directly.

slides.title: Welcoming someone new
slides.text: Being new at a school is nerve-wracking, so going out of your way to say hi really matters. Sitting with a new student at lunch can turn their scary first day around.

slides.title: A sincere apology
slides.text: A real apology names what you did wrong and how you'll do better next time. That means a lot more than a quick 'sorry' said while walking away.

slides.title: Staying friends even when apart
slides.text: Friendships can survive time apart, like summer break, if you make a little effort to stay in touch. A quick message just to say hi can keep a friendship strong.

slides.title: Handling jealousy
slides.text: Feeling jealous when a friend does something great is normal, but acting mean about it can hurt the friendship. Noticing the feeling and cheering for them anyway is the stronger choice.

slides.title: Making friends in a new place
slides.text: Moving to a new school or neighborhood can feel scary, but most kids are open to a new friend. Joining a club or team is an easy way to meet people who like the same things.

slides.title: Including someone who's left out
slides.text: If you notice someone eating alone or standing by themselves, inviting them over takes just a moment. That small choice can turn a lonely day into a much better one.

slides.title: Being a good listener
slides.text: A good listener asks questions and remembers what their friend told them before. Really paying attention, instead of thinking about what to say next, makes a friend feel valued.

slides.title: Being yourself vs. fitting in
slides.text: Trying to act like a completely different person just to be liked usually backfires — the friendships that last are the ones where people like the real you. For example, pretending to love a hobby you actually don't just to fit in with a group might work short-term, but it's exhausting and doesn't lead to a genuine friendship.

slides.title: Navigating cliques
slides.text: Groups of friends (cliques) can feel exclusive sometimes — you can be friendly with a group without needing to be best friends with every single person in it. For example, being kind to everyone in a friend group, even people you're not especially close to, keeps things comfortable without pressuring you to be equally close to all of them.

slides.title: Supporting a friend through something hard
slides.text: When a friend is going through something difficult, like their parents' divorce or a tough loss, just being there and listening usually helps more than trying to fix it. For example, sitting with a friend and letting them talk about a hard time, without immediately jumping to advice, often helps them feel less alone.

slides.title: Dealing with jealousy
slides.text: Feeling a little jealous when a friend does something great isn't unusual, but acting on that jealousy can hurt the friendship — noticing the feeling and choosing kindness anyway matters. For example, feeling a twinge of jealousy when a friend makes a team you didn't, but still congratulating them sincerely, protects the friendship even though the feeling is uncomfortable.

slides.title: Friendships that drift apart
slides.text: Sometimes friends grow apart naturally as interests change, and that's a normal part of growing up, not something that means you did anything wrong. For example, a childhood best friend moving toward different hobbies and a different friend group over a couple of years doesn't mean either of you failed at friendship — people just change.

slides.title: Online friendships
slides.text: Friends made through games or apps can be real friendships, but it's worth being extra careful about sharing personal details with people you've never met in person. For example, having a great time playing an online game with someone doesn't mean it's safe to share your home address or school name with them.

slides.title: Standing up for a friend
slides.text: If someone is being unkind to a friend, speaking up — even just saying 'that's not okay' — shows real loyalty, even when it feels a little scary. For example, telling a group 'that's not cool, leave them alone' when they're teasing a friend takes courage but can mean everything to the friend being defended.

slides.title: Balancing multiple friend groups
slides.text: Having friends in different groups — like school, a sports team, and a hobby — is completely normal, and you don't owe any one group all of your time. For example, splitting your weekend between a school friend and a teammate, instead of feeling guilty for not spending all your time with just one group, is a healthy way to have a bigger, more varied social life.

slides.title: Making new friends after a move
slides.text: Starting over at a new school or in a new neighborhood can feel intimidating, but most people are more open to new friends than it seems. For example, joining a club, a team, or even just sitting with a friendly-looking group at lunch during your first week can turn an awkward transition into the start of a real friendship.

slides.title: Saying sorry and meaning it
slides.text: A real apology isn't just about avoiding an awkward silence — it means acknowledging what you did, how it affected your friend, and actually changing the behavior going forward. For example, saying 'I'm sorry I canceled last minute again, I'll give you more notice next time' means a lot more than a quick, vague 'my bad.'

slides.title: Including someone who's often left out
slides.text: Noticing that one person keeps getting left off invites or out of group chats, and making a small effort to include them, can mean more than you'd expect. For example, adding someone to a group project or inviting them along even once can change how included they feel for a long time, even if they never say so directly.

slides.title: Being a good listener, not just a good talker
slides.text: Really listening means asking follow-up questions and remembering details, instead of just waiting for your turn to talk about yourself. For example, a friend who remembers you had a big test this week and asks how it went, without being reminded, is practicing the kind of listening that makes people feel truly cared about.

quiz.explanation: Genuine friendships tend to be built on authenticity, not a performance.

choices: Acknowledging what happened and actually changing your behavior
Saying 'my bad' quickly and moving on

Waiting for your turn to talk about yourself
quiz.explanation: Attentive listening, not just hearing, is what makes a friend feel valued.

slides.title: Authentic vs. surface-level friendships
slides.text: Some friendships stay surface-level — fun but not deep — while others grow into real trust over time; both have their place, but knowing the difference helps you invest your energy well. For example, someone you only ever talk to about school gossip is a different kind of friend than someone you'd call at 2am with a real problem — both are valid, but they're not the same.

slides.title: Mutual respect and boundaries
slides.text: A healthy friendship respects that both people have limits — like needing space sometimes, or not wanting to discuss certain topics — without taking it personally. For example, a friend saying 'I need some space this weekend' isn't a rejection; respecting that request without guilt-tripping them is part of a mature friendship.

slides.title: Repairing a friendship after conflict
slides.text: Not every disagreement has to end a friendship — a real conversation about what happened, without rehashing every old grievance, can often repair things. For example, having one honest, calm conversation about a specific fight — instead of avoiding each other for weeks — often clears the air faster than either person expects.

slides.title: Recognizing toxic patterns
slides.text: A friend who constantly puts you down, only reaches out when they need something, or makes you feel worse after hanging out is showing a pattern worth paying attention to. For example, noticing that you consistently feel drained or anxious after spending time with a specific person — rather than just having one bad day — is worth taking seriously.

slides.title: Long-distance friendships
slides.text: Friendships can survive moving away or going to different schools, but they usually need more intentional effort — a call, a message, a visit — since you won't just run into each other anymore. For example, scheduling a regular video call with a friend who moved away, instead of hoping you'll naturally stay in touch, keeps a long-distance friendship genuinely alive.

slides.title: Resisting pressure to exclude someone
slides.text: Peer pressure to leave someone out or join in on unkind behavior can be hard to resist, but choosing not to participate — even quietly — matters. For example, not joining in when a group starts excluding or mocking someone, even if you don't openly object, is a meaningful choice not to add to the harm.

slides.title: Growing in different directions
slides.text: As people figure out who they are during the teen years, some friendships naturally fade — that's a normal part of growing, not a personal failure on either side. For example, two friends who were inseparable in middle school discovering very different interests and friend groups by the end of high school is a common, normal part of growing up.

slides.title: Vulnerability deepens friendship
slides.text: Sharing something real — a worry, a fear, an honest opinion — is often what turns a casual friendship into a close one, even though it feels risky. For example, admitting to a friend that you're actually nervous about an upcoming decision, instead of pretending everything's fine, often brings you closer rather than pushing them away.

slides.title: Being reliable under pressure
slides.text: A real test of friendship is whether you show up for someone even when it's inconvenient or a little uncomfortable, not just when it's easy. For example, going to support a friend at a hard event, even though you'd rather be somewhere else that night, is the kind of reliability that real friendships are built on.

slides.title: Handling jealousy without damaging trust
slides.text: Feeling a flicker of jealousy when a friend succeeds at something you wanted for yourself is normal — the difference between a healthy friendship and a strained one is often what you do with that feeling. For example, privately acknowledging you feel a little envious, while still congratulating your friend sincerely, keeps the friendship intact instead of letting an unspoken resentment quietly build up.

slides.title: Being present: the power of good listening
slides.text: Really listening — putting your phone down, asking questions, and not planning your response while the other person is still talking — is one of the most underrated ways to deepen a friendship. For example, a friend who remembers a hard conversation from weeks ago and checks in about it, unprompted, is showing a kind of attentiveness that most casual friendships never reach.

slides.title: Including someone who's new or on the outside
slides.text: Actively including someone who's new, quiet, or often left on the edge of a group takes a small amount of effort but can change how they experience an entire year. For example, texting someone you don't know well to invite them along, instead of assuming they'll ask to join, is a simple way to make a group feel more open.

slides.title: Making friends outside your usual circle
slides.text: As your interests and identity keep developing through your teen years, some of your best friendships might come from outside your usual friend group — a club, a job, or a shared interest online. For example, a genuine friendship with someone from a completely different social circle can offer a perspective and support that your closer, more similar friends might not.
